newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Arrest sought for S.Korean MPs over loan scandal - TV.
newsitem.headline: Arrest sought for S.Korean MPs over loan scandal - TV.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors plan to seek arrest warrants for two ruling party members of parliament, including a close associate of President Kim Young-sam, over a loan scandal, Yonhap Television News reported on Tuesday.

A prosecution official said prosecutors were questioning Hong In-gil, a senior official at the presidential Blue House until last year, and Chung Jae-chull in connection with huge loans to Hanbo Steel Co.
"But no decision has been made on whether to seek arrest warrants against the two deputies," the official told Reuters.

The prosecutors on Monday summoned Hong and Chung, who is a top official of Kim's New Korea Party, to determine if they accepted kickbacks from Hanbo Steel and pressured bankers into offering loans to the company.
"The prosecution plans to seek arrest warrants for the two lawmakers today," the television said.

The two are the first politicians to be probed over loans totalling five trillion won ($5.8 billion) provided to Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, before it was declared insolvent on January 23.
President Kim, who last month ordered a probe into the loans, has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.

The prosecutors, who have already arrested Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo and two leading bankers over the loans, also questioned the tycoon's driver on Tuesday on suspicions of carrying big boxes stuffed with cash to bankers and politicians, the prosecution official said.
"The driver was a Hanbo executive in charge of protocol. We hope he could shed more light to the case," he added.
The prosecutors have also summoned Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, but two main opposition groups on Tuesday urged him not to report to the prosecution office.

"The prosecutors are trying to implicate the opposition to whitewash the nature of the Hanbo incident while trying to cover up real power behind the scene," spokesman Yun Ho-jung of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics told Reuters.
Kwon, who earlier said he would report to prosecutors on Tuesday, said he would now wait until the prosecutors served him an official summons. Kwon was ealier summoned by telephone.
National Congress and the United Liberal Democratic Party, which together control 123 of the 299 seats in parliament, have accused top government officials of peddling influence for the loans.

They alleged that the government's favour allowed Hanbo Group to emerge as South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate by rapidly expanding its steelmaking flagship and by acquiring or setting up 18 firms over the past three years.
Hong, who has been President Kim's aide for more than two decades, has denied taking money from Hanbo.
Kwon, a leading National Congress member, said he had nothing to do with Hanbo loans. But he has said he took between 150 million and 160 million won from Hanbo, partly to fund an election campaign.
The other lawmaker has not publicly commented. ($ = 867.80 won)
